## Research Question

::: {.r-hstack}

![Learning Putonghua](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/speak_policy.jpg){height=360}

!["Support Cantonese"](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7c/Support_Cantonese_20100725.jpg){height=360}

:::

::: {.fragment style="text-align:center"}

*Does the language a state [governs]{.red} change how citizens see the state?*

::: {.fragment}

> "What matters is the **content** a language carries, not the language itself."

:::

:::

::: {.notes}

Open with the objection. When I started this project, the most common reaction from friends was exactly this: what matters is the content a language carries and how it is said, not the language itself. I will come back to it at the end.

On February 4, 2009, a local newspaper labelled speaking Shanghainese a mark of being uneducated, and prominent figures pushed back at once. In 2010 a proposal at the Guangzhou Political Consultative Conference to use only Putonghua in prime-time news met resistance and even public demonstrations. Mother-tongue protection movements also appeared in Sichuan, Shaanxi, and Beijing.

Yet at the same time 80.72 percent of the population is proficient in Putonghua, and parents worry about their children's Putonghua from birth. Local mother-tongue protection alongside national Putonghua prevalence: that tension is where the book begins.

Right photo: the "Support Cantonese" gathering in Guangzhou on 25 July 2010, protesting a proposal to increase Putonghua broadcasting on Guangzhou Television. Paul Wong, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Support_Cantonese_20100725.jpg

:::

# The Official Language Field

## Language, Humans, and Politics

::: {.r-fit-text}

> The human "autapomorphy" [@BerwickChomsky2016]

:::

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}

**Linguistic relativity: language shapes thought**

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/speak_linguisticRelativity_gender.png){fig-align="center" height=260}

- Different mother tongues &rarr; different [basic cognition]{.red}
- Time, space, color, gender

:::

::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}

**Language policy: language marks ethnicity**

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/process_singaporeLang.jpg){fig-align="center" height=260}

- Balancing ethnic groups, building identity
- A tool of state and ethnic governance

:::

::::

::: {.notes}

Evolutionary biologists call language a human autapomorphy, a trait unique to our species [@BerwickChomsky2016, p. 54].

Left, linguistic relativity: speakers of different languages differ in basic cognitive domains like time, space, color, and gender. The grammatical gender of sun, moon, and bridge differs between German and Spanish, and speakers' adjectives follow. A bridge is feminine in German, so "beautiful, elegant"; masculine in Spanish, so "strong, long".

These findings stay in basic cognition. The book asks three questions. Can language also shape more complex political mindsets, such as perceptions of political authority or the government-mass relationship? If so, is it the language itself or the content it conveys? And what role does political authority play: can it create, modify, or mitigate these effects?

Right, language policy research: a four-language "No Loitering" sign in Singapore, which recognizes English, Chinese, Malay, and Tamil. This line of work explains why and how states pursue language policies, through political economy and state building [@Liu2015], but says less about what those policies do to the mass population once in place.

:::

## Existing Theories

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="47%"}

**Linguistic relativity**

- Mother tongue shapes [perception]{.red}
- Language exogenous and fixed

:::

::: {.column .fragment width="53%"}

**Language as identity**

- Language marks [ethnic]{.red} membership
- Acculturation &rarr; align with the dominant group
- Ethnic competition &rarr; opposite pull

:::

::::

::: {.callout-note .fragment}

## Three Blind Spots

1. Language [learning]{.red} underweighted
2. Non-identity variance ignored
3. Holistic measures &rarr; risk of a [Type S error]{.red} [@GelmanCarlin2014]

:::

::: {.notes}

Both branches treat language holistically, as a proxy for culture or for group membership. That holistic view is what keeps the field from asking whether different language functions, listening versus speaking versus relative standing, do different political work.

The acculturation model expects that using the dominant language pulls people toward the dominant group and its authority; the ethnic competition model expects the opposite. Both are identity stories.

A Type S error is a sign error: with a holistic measure, two functions that push in opposite directions can cancel, and the estimated sign can come out wrong.

Language has long sat at the margins of political science; Laitin raised the concern back in 1988 [@Laitin1988]. The "content" view from the opening is the other rival: it treats language as a mere channel. The evidence will answer both.

:::

## The Official Language Field (OLF)

- Official language defined by [practice]{.red}, not legal recognition
- Habitually used by the authority in political affairs &rarr; the [voice of the state]{.red}
- Field: the [habitual hierarchy]{.red} of language use in public affairs
- Two layers: the official language over dialects, minority and foreign languages
- Functional view [@LaitinRamachandran2016] &rarr; add [power]{.red}

::: {.notes}

Canada recognizes two official languages, Singapore four, and some U.S. states one or more, yet in each a single language dominates political practice. China has never legally declared Putonghua an official language; the laws call it the "nationally common language". The practical definition is what makes the theory portable.

Political linguists have recently moved toward the functional properties of language rather than cultural identity. OLF builds on that shift and highlights the political dimension of language functions.

:::

::: {.r-fit-text .fragment style="text-align:center; margin-top: 1em"}

&rArr; One language: [three functions, three directions]{.red}

:::

## Three Mechanisms

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/theoryDiagram.png){fig-align="center" height=420}

:::

::: {.column width="45%"}

**Exposure**: rides on [listening]{.red}

- Information intake + authority evocation

**Expression**: rides on [speaking]{.red}

- Externalizing demands and opinions

**Competition**: rides on [relative proficiency]{.red}

- Advantage over local peers

:::

::::

::: {.callout-important .fragment}

## Hypotheses

- H<sub>1</sub>: Listening [&uarr;]{.blue} &rarr; knowledge, compliance [&uarr;]{.blue} &rarr; trust [&uarr;]{.blue}
- H<sub>2</sub>: Speaking [&uarr;]{.blue} &rarr; internal efficacy [&uarr;]{.blue}, external efficacy [&darr;]{.red} &rarr; trust [&darr;]{.red}
- H<sub>3</sub>: Relative proficiency [&uarr;]{.blue} &rarr; gratification, standing [&uarr;]{.blue} &rarr; trust [&uarr;]{.blue}

:::

::: {.notes}

The three mechanisms overlap in practice; the claim is that each has a distinct primary domain.

Relative proficiency is an individual's speaking proficiency minus the average in their prefecture. A modest speaker in a low-proficiency county can hold a larger advantage than a strong speaker in Shanghai.

Internal efficacy is confidence in one's own ability to understand and take part in politics; external efficacy is the belief that government responds to people like oneself. High internal with low external is the combination the literature links to falling trust.

H1 is stated for the central government. Hierarchical trust theory expects central and local trust to move in opposite directions in China.

The divergence is what separates OLF from the ethnolinguistic account: if language worked holistically as a proxy for culture, the three functions should not diverge in sign.

:::

# The Official Language Field in China

## Building a "Tower of Babel"

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="45%"}

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/speak_policy.jpg){fig-align="center" height=420}

:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

- 1955: [Putonghua]{.red} defined as the national standard
- 1956: Central Working Committee for the Promotion of Putonghua
- 1958: *Scheme for Chinese Phonetic Writing*; Pinyin enters schools
- Promotion of Putonghua written into the [Constitution]{.red}
- 2000: *Law on the Standard Spoken and Written Chinese Language*
- 2022: National Language and Script Promotion Bases

:::

::::

::: {.notes}

The 1955 conferences created Putonghua: the vocabulary and grammar of Northern Mandarin with Beijing pronunciation as the standard. In 1958 the Ministry of Education mandated Pinyin and Putonghua in primary, middle, and teacher-training schools.

Promotion then entered education law (Kindergarten Regulations 1989, Education Law 1995, Compulsory Education Law 2006) and broadcasting rules; even portrayals of the PRC's founding figures were aligned to standard Putonghua despite their well-known dialects. The 2000 law was the PRC's first dedicated legislative act on language.

In the biblical allegory, divine intervention introduced linguistic diversity to curb human ambition. Secular authorities do the opposite: they seek power security by promoting a unified official language, and China is no exception.

<!-- [Check] Constitution year: the book (Ch. 1) says 1985, but the provision is usually dated to Article 19 of the 1982 Constitution. Left off the slide until confirmed -->

:::

## Case Selection: China

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

![Language](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/speak_chineseLanguage.png){fig-align="center" height=380}

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

![Ethnicity](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/speak_chineseEthnicity.png){fig-align="center" height=380}

:::

::::

- About [200]{.red} living dialects, one dominant official language
- Linguistic map does [not]{.red} track the ethnic map &rarr; separate language from ethnicity
- Six decades of consistent promotion &rarr; observable direction and size of effects

::: {.notes}

Left is the linguistic distribution, right the ethnic one. China's linguistic system is discernibly more diverse than its ethnic system. The Han majority speaks various dialects; some are regional, such as Sichuanese and Tianjinese, others cross regions, such as Cantonese and Hakka. Many ethnic minorities also speak Putonghua.

This heterogeneity lets us discern the influence of language independent of ethnic or geographic factors. Applying OLF only requires two prerequisites: a multilingual society and an identifiable official language.

:::

## Putonghua Proficiency

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/speak_profYear.png){fig-align="center" height=250}

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

- [80.72%]{.red} proficient, but levels vary widely
- Listening consistently [exceeds]{.red} speaking across waves
- Large provincial variation

:::

::::

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/speak_avgMap.png){fig-align="center" height=400 .fragment}

::: {.notes}

According to the latest statistics, 80.72 percent of the population, roughly 1.1 of 1.4 billion people, is proficient in Putonghua, and over 95 percent use simplified characters. But being able to use it is not the same as using it equally well: across CGSS waves, self-rated listening always exceeds speaking, and provincial averages differ widely.

That is OLF's starting point: the effects lie not in whether people know the language but in how well, and in which function.

:::

## Proficiency Is Not a Proxy

::: {.r-stack}

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/speak_indFactors.png){fig-align="center" height=480}

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/speak_provFactors.png){.fragment fig-align="center" height=480}

:::

- Individual and provincial factors explain only [30%]{.red} of listening and [50%]{.red} of speaking variance

::: {.notes}

First the individual-level determinants, then the provincial ones.

Most factors point the same way with different magnitudes. Migrants and minorities differ: once other factors are held constant, ethnic minorities show lower listening but higher speaking proficiency than Han.

Cragg and Uhler's pseudo R-squared shows that individual and group factors together account for only about 30 percent of the variance in listening and 50 percent in speaking. Putonghua proficiency is far more than a proxy for education, ethnicity, or geography. This is the pre-emptive answer to "isn't proficiency just education?"

:::

# Effects and Mechanisms

## Research Design

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Data**

- Chinese General Social Survey (CGSS), 2010–2015
- N = 17,664, 31 provinces
- Trust battery: [2010]{.red} only

:::

::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}

**Measures**

- Listening, speaking: self-rated, 1–5
- Relative proficiency: $\Delta_{s_{ik}} = s_{ik} - \bar{s}_k$
- Outcomes: knowledge, compliance, efficacy, standing, trust

:::

::::

::: {.fragment}

*Strategy*

- Three functions raced against each other in [one model]{.red}
- Multilevel models + GAM; controls for education, ethnicity, income, party membership, and more

:::

::: {.notes}

Multistage stratified PPS sampling, nationally representative. Relative proficiency is the individual's speaking score minus the prefecture mean, the prefecture being the smallest geographic unit the CGSS reports.

Efficacy items run in 2010 and 2012; the political trust battery was asked only in 2010, so the trust models are cross-sectional. Generalized multilevel models with provincial varying intercepts and wave fixed effects; generalized additive models as a sensitivity check for nonlinear control effects. Controls: education, age, ethnic identity, gender, family income, party membership, media habits, occupation type.

On causal direction: language learning precedes political learning, which leaves little room for reverse causation. The experiment that follows tests the listening effect under random assignment.

:::

## Effects: Political Cognition

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/speak_listen.png){fig-align="center"}

*Exposure*

- Listening [&uarr;]{.blue} &rarr; political knowledge [&uarr;]{.blue}
- Compliance [&uarr;]{.blue}
- Opposes what the state restricts, favors what it promotes

:::

::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/speak_speak.png){fig-align="center"}

*Expression*

- Speaking [&uarr;]{.blue} &rarr; internal efficacy [&uarr;]{.blue}
- External efficacy [&darr;]{.red}
- More will to take part vs. less faith in being heard

:::

::::

::: {.notes}

Political knowledge: whether the respondent could name the current Speaker of the National People's Congress. Compliance: a graded response IRT score from reported compliance with rules ranging from traffic laws to policy regulations. The restricted affair was laissez-faire birth; the promoted one was population mobility.

:::

## Effects: Competition

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/speak_relative.png){fig-align="center" width="90%"}

- Relative proficiency [&uarr;]{.blue} &rarr; gratification [&uarr;]{.blue}: against peers and against three years ago
- Self-assessed social standing [&uarr;]{.blue}, perceived fairness [&uarr;]{.blue}
- Where one [excels]{.red} linguistically, one embraces the established order

::: {.notes}

Data: the CGSS 2013 socioeconomic gratification module (horizontal comparison with peers, vertical comparison with oneself three years earlier) and the MacArthur social ladder in CGSS 2015.

Those whose Putonghua beats their local peers' are more likely to recognize their advantage and report more gratification, standing, and fairness. This sets up the trust result: they should trust the government that creates and maintains the linguistic environment in which they excel.

:::

## Effects: Political Trust

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="58%"}

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/speak_trust.png){fig-align="center" height=600}

:::

::: {.column width="42%"}

- Listening &rarr; central trust [&uarr;]{.blue}, local trust [&darr;]{.red}
- Speaking &rarr; central and NPC trust [&darr;]{.red}
- Relative proficiency &rarr; central and NPC trust [&uarr;]{.blue}
- Ethnic identity: [no effect at the national level]{.grayLight}

[*[Different functions of one language push political minds in opposite directions]{.red}*]{.fragment}

:::

::::

::: {.notes}

The key slide. Slow down.

Listening to central trust is inconclusive at .05 under the multilevel model but positive and significant under GAM, and confirmed by trust in the NPC, the robustness measure of central trust. The negative local coefficient matches hierarchical trust theory.

Relative proficiency carries the largest coefficient on national trust, surpassing education, income, and partisanship.

The null on ethnic identity is what the ethnolinguistic account cannot accommodate: once the functional effects of proficiency are held constant, being a minority does not predict national political trust.

On the "content" objection: if content were all that mattered, listening and speaking in the same language should not diverge. Speaking Putonghua is an oral skill; getting information online is mostly reading. They are not the same channel.

One policy, a more compliant and a more critical citizenry at once.

:::

## From Effect to Mechanism

> Does the official language itself call the [authority]{.red} to mind?

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Design**

- Adjusted matched-guise experiment, double blind [@Hu2020]
- Two scenarios: complaint response, recrimination
- Same bilingual speakers, identical scripts
- Only the second speaker's language varies

:::

::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}

**Subjects**

- 421 high school students
- Chengdu, speaking Sichuanese
- Meizhou, speaking Hakka
- Two dialects, two distances from Putonghua

:::

::::

::: {.fragment}

**Measures**: trustworthy (trust game), authentic, close

:::

::: {.notes}

Surveys show the outcome, not the evocation. The experiment fills that gap.

Classic matched-guise has each listener hear the same speaker twice in two languages, which hurts ecological validity and telegraphs the purpose. The adjustment randomizes listeners into groups that hear only one version, after realistic background information. In the trust game, participants decide how many coins to transfer to the speaker. Sichuanese is partly intelligible with Putonghua while Hakka is distant, so the pair tests whether the finding depends on one dialect.

High school students limit external validity; random assignment secures internal validity.

:::

## Experimental Scenarios

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

![Complaint response](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/listen_response.jpg){fig-align="center" height=320}

- Noise complaint &rarr; property office, construction committee reply

:::

::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}

![Recrimination](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/listen_recrimination.jpg){fig-align="center" height=320}

- Breakfast vendor vs. urban management officer

:::

::::

::: {.fragment style="text-align:center"}

Each group hears [one language]{.red} version &rarr; attitudes toward the second speaker

:::

::: {.notes}

Fielded December 2016 to January 2017.

Complaint response: a classmate's family lives above a shop whose central air-conditioning compressor produces noise beyond the legal limit. The parent calls the 12345 citizen hotline and is passed first to a public servant at the City Department of Property Management, then to an official from the Municipal Construction Committee.

Recrimination: a breakfast vendor complains about an urban management officer's enforcement, and the two argue.

Participants learn the speakers' identities first, then hear the recording once, in one language only. That hides the purpose and keeps subjects from overstating language preferences. The second speaker, the government agent, is the focus.

:::

## The Authority Marker

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/listen_avg.png){fig-align="center" height=400}

- Trustworthy [&uarr;]{.blue}
- Authentic [&uarr;]{.grayLight}
- Close [&uarr;]{.blue} (complaint response)
- Chance of being classed as distrustful falls by over [10%]{.red}

::: {.notes}

Results hold with and without controls for gender, length of local residence, family socioeconomic status, general interpersonal trust, and dialect proficiency, and with a site fixed effect. Authenticity is tentative at .05.

:::

## Reducing Distrust

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/listen_distrust.png){fig-align="center" height=420}

:::

::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/listen_marginOfficial.png){fig-align="center" height=420}

:::

::::

- Putonghua raises the chance of clearing trust thresholds [&uarr;]{.blue} (two of six [null]{.grayLight})
- Strongest among those who [distrusted]{.red} the speaker to begin with

::: {.notes}

Left: trust split at thresholds; Putonghua raises the probability of clearing them in four of six tests. Right: first differences in predicted probability, Putonghua versus vernacular.

For regime stability, pulling the distrustful back matters more than turning moderate trust into high trust, and that is exactly where the authority marker works hardest.

:::

## Placebo: Take Away the Badge

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/listen_mass.png){fig-align="center" height=340}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="60%"}

Same speakers, same two languages, no government identity

- General trust: [no difference]{.grayLight}
- Authenticity: [no difference]{.grayLight}
- Closeness: toward the [vernacular]{.red}

:::

::: {.column .fragment width="40%"}

::: {style="text-align:center; margin-top: 3em"}

*Political identity is the [switch]{.red}:*

*without it, the culture marker returns*

:::

:::

::::

::: {.notes}

Replacement scenarios: a friend recommending a mobile phone, and two private drivers arguing after a near miss. No political role.

The strongest single piece of evidence: the effect runs through the language-authority connection, not through Putonghua as a marker of education or urban origin. The content did not change either; only the language did. And the ethnolinguistic account is not wrong, it is conditional.

:::

# Other Languages in the Field

## English in China

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/foreign_proficiency.png){fig-align="center" height=400}

:::

::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/foreign_geo.png){fig-align="center" height=400}

:::

::::

- In the national language education plan since 1964; compulsory in the college entrance exam since 1983
- Over [400 million]{.red} learners, about a third of the population
- Low average proficiency (about 1.5 of 5); listening above speaking

::: {.notes}

Since 2001 primary schools generally start English in the third grade, earlier in Beijing and Shanghai. English learners now outnumber the speakers of any dialect.

English has arguably transcended its status as a skill and become a signal of education and learning capability. That matters: it gives English a competition channel comparable to Putonghua's.

:::

## English: A Control without Endorsement

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/foreign_direct.png){fig-align="center" height=420}

:::

::: {.column width="45%"}

- **Shared**: state promotion, exam requirement, 400 million learners
- **Missing**: never [endorsed]{.red} as the voice of the state
- Listening &rarr; efficacy [&uarr;]{.blue}, central trust [&darr;]{.red}
- Speaking &rarr; efficacy [&uarr;]{.blue}, [trust unaffected]{.grayLight}
- Paths: information and competition, [not values]{.grayLight}

:::

::::

::: {.notes}

The state pushed English through the education system as hard as Putonghua but never speaks to citizens in English. English therefore removes the endorsement variable while roughly holding the education channel constant.

Same function, listening: Putonghua raises central trust, English lowers it. The substantive difference is political endorsement.

Two caveats to concede before anyone asks. First, the two sides come from different estimators (kernel regularized least squares on CGSS 2010 for English), so this is a comparison across analyses, not a single interaction test. Second, English is also a signal of ability, so the contrast is suggestive.

:::

## English: Pathways

::: {.r-stack}

::: {layout-ncol=2}

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/plot_listen2internal.png){height=240}

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/plot_listen2external.png){height=240}

:::

::: {.fragment layout-ncol=2}

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/plot_speak2internal.png){height=240}

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/plot_speak2external.png){height=240}

:::

::: {.fragment layout-ncol=2}

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/plot_listen2trust.png){height=240}

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/plot_speak2trust.png){height=240}

:::

:::

- Efficacy: information collection + competitive advantage; [no value path]{.grayLight}
- Trust: every identified path positive, direct effect [negative]{.red}

::: {.notes}

Causal mediation analysis following Imai et al., which rests on sequential ignorability; the book reports sensitivity tests. Cross-sectional data, so do not place too much causal weight here.

Internal efficacy: listening works mainly through Internet-based information collection; speaking has information collection as its only identifiable path. External efficacy: listening runs through self-assessed status and relative proficiency, the latter ten times larger; speaking only through relative proficiency.

Attitude toward freedom of speech was tested as a value mediator and carries nothing. Learning English does not make people more Western in values; it shapes behavior over values [@HuYueZhuMeng2022].

Trust: the identified paths are positive, yet the direct effect is significantly negative. The mechanisms do not explain the negative sign. An open puzzle.

:::

## Dialects: Still Spoken

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/migrant_langDist.png){fig-align="center" height=480}

- Residents: the vernacular is the top choice at work; over [80%]{.red} use it after work
- Migrants: the local vernacular is still the [modal]{.red} after-work choice (about 40%)

::: {.notes}

China Labor-Force Dynamics Survey 2016 asked which language respondents use during and after working hours: only the local vernacular, only Putonghua, both, or only their own native dialect.

After work, more than 80 percent of residents use the vernacular, three times those choosing Putonghua. Most migrants use Putonghua at work, but over a quarter also use the vernacular; after work about 40 percent use the local vernacular, about 10 points more than Putonghua or their native dialect. Notwithstanding claims that Putonghua is replacing vernaculars, the vernacular is still favored.

:::

## Dialects and Migration: Stated vs. Revealed [@HuPizzi2022]

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/migrant_experiment.png){fig-align="center" height=380}

- Stated: economics first; [few]{.red} mention language
- Survey experiment: hold the income gap, vary only the language barrier
- About [10%]{.red} shift toward the city with the closer dialect
- Migrant status, gender, education: [no moderation]{.grayLight}

::: {.notes}

Data: Living Environment Satisfaction Survey (LESS 2018), 1,100 respondents across all 31 provinces, half of them migrants, with gender and education matching the census.

In every condition City A pays more than City B; in the treatment, A's local dialect is less intelligible. In the control over 45 percent are "more likely" to choose A and over 25 percent "definitely" would. Adding the language condition cuts those groups by about 10 and 5 percent, and about 10 percent more lean to B.

Language shapes the decision below the level of stated reasons.

:::

## Dialects and Migration: Bypass, Not Erase

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/book_migrant_bypass.png){fig-align="center" height=600}

:::

::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}

- Putonghua [&uarr;]{.blue} &rarr; willingness to stay [&uarr;]{.blue}, without learning the vernacular
  - Threshold: positive only once Putonghua allows basic communication
  - Language barrier still significant &rarr; Putonghua [bypasses]{.red}, not erases, the dialect
- Dialects: identity and social capital &rarr; [coexist]{.red} with Putonghua

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/book_migrant_threshold.png){fig-align="center" height=250}

:::

::::

::: {.notes}

Data: CLDS 2016.

Left (Fig. 5.5, bypass effect): nonlinear ordered logit. Migrants with better Putonghua are more willing to remain in destination cities, yet the language barrier measures stay significant and in the same direction. Putonghua provides an additional communicative tool but does not eliminate cultural concerns.

Right (Fig. 5.6, threshold effect): a regression discontinuity at "barely speaking". Below the threshold the effect leans negative but is inconclusive; above it, positive and significant.

Implication: in an official language field each language does its own work. The dialect's work is cultural, which also bears on migration and hukou policy.

:::

# Political Linguistics as a [Research Agenda]{.red}

## Beyond Listening and Speaking: Democracy in Writing [@Hu2020a]

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Problem**

- Reading-writing hard to separate from [education]{.red}
- Detour: study the discourse itself

**Data**

- *People's Daily*, five decades, over a million articles
- Computer-assisted text analysis

:::

::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}

**Finding: a [refocusing]{.red} strategy**

- Within discourse: democracy defined by national priorities
- Across discourse: published alongside liberal values
- Payoff: support for democracy and for the regime [coexist]{.red}

:::

::::

::: {.notes}

A developed literature shows that Chinese citizens understand democracy in ways both representative of Asia and distinct from the West, and that they support democracy while also supporting the established regime. Chapter 7 offers a political linguistic explanation.

The refocusing strategy sidesteps direct conflict with the globally prevalent liberal understanding of democracy and redirects the definition toward national development and achievement, areas where the regime excels. The pattern holds across periods and international conditions. It speaks to the soft propaganda literature: subtle framing can outperform hard-line indoctrination, and can run for decades.

<!-- [Suggest] Text-only slide. Candidates: the 1991 discourse network graph from democracy.qmd chunk `networkPlot`, or the `fig-withinCross` coefficient panel (needs a ggsave export) -->

:::

## Beyond China

- Two prerequisites: a [multilingual society]{.red} + an identifiable official language
- France: promotion since the 16th century, nationwide policy in 1794
- Russia, Bangladesh, Nepal, Germany
- De facto official languages: United States, United Kingdom, Australia
- After state building, language policy [still]{.red} shapes political minds

::: {.notes}

The practical definition of official language is what makes the theory travel; it does not require a particular legal arrangement. Where policies differ, the three mechanisms still apply, but predicted directions may change with local conditions.

Modernization theory [Inglehart and Woodward 1967] expects three phases: unification builds allegiance to a new nation; a developed society then demands linguistic diversity; finally perceived barriers fall and policy loses relevance. In China the second and third phases overlap. Most citizens have mastered Putonghua, yet attachment to the vernaculars persists, so language policy keeps shaping the whole population instead of fading out.

:::

## Why a Research Agenda

| Condition | Objection | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Is the effect separable? | "It's the content" | Listening and speaking diverge; same content, different language, different trust |
| Where does it come from? | "Language only marks identity" | Authority marker needs "government identity + Putonghua"; English flips the sign; dialects do cultural work |
| Can it be identified? | "Only long-term, subtle effects" | National surveys, lab and survey experiments, large-scale text |

::: {.r-fit-text .fragment style="text-align:center; margin-top: 1em"}

[*Language is more than a carrier of content:*]{.red}

[*the authority's ranking gives it political force that can be isolated, theorized, and identified*]{.red}

:::

::: {.notes}

Back to the opening objection: what matters is the content, not the language?

First, in the experiment the content was fixed and only the language changed, yet trust changed; in the survey the same language's listening and speaking diverge, which a content account cannot explain. Second, the source is not culture: the authority marker needs a government identity, and without it the culture marker returns; English is promoted but not endorsed, and the same function flips sign. Third, these conclusions come from different data and designs that converge. Each design rests on its own assumptions: the surveys on no omitted confounding, the experiment on successful randomization, the mediation on sequential ignorability, and English doubles as a signal of ability. But they point the same way.

On "only long-term, subtle effects": the lab experiment moved trust with a single hearing of one recording.

:::

## A Linguistic Turn in Political Science

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Where language has sat**

- Peripheral in political science [@Laitin1988]
- Studied as a [policy outcome]{.red}: why states standardize [@Liu2015]
- Or as a proxy for ethnicity and culture

:::

::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}

**Where it can go**

- Language as an [explanatory variable]{.red} and a political resource
- Functional effects [@LaitinRamachandran2016]
- Opinion and cognition [@Perez2015; @PerezTavits2017]

:::

::::

::: {.fragment style="text-align:center; margin-top: 1em"}

An interdisciplinary route linking psychology, linguistics, sociology, communication, economics, and data science

:::

::: {.notes}

Although Laitin raised concerns about this omission last century, language still frequently occupies a peripheral role in political science. Political linguistics has nonetheless kept exploring language effects and increasingly borrows interdisciplinary perspectives and methods. OLF aims to show how broad language policies shape detailed political cognition.

:::

## Open Questions

- Language policy &rarr; interpersonal trust, perceived inequality?
- Dialect protection &rarr; how does it change policy effects?
- Foreign language learning &rarr; undiscovered mechanisms?
- Where does English's [negative direct effect]{.red} on trust come from?

::: {.fragment}

> [Some of language's most significant effects occur at a deep, automatic level, influencing what is initially activated in memory.]{.red}

:::{style="text-align:right"}

[--- @Perez2015, p. 266]{.red}

:::

:::

::: {.notes}

The first three come from the book's conclusion; the fourth is the unexplained result of the English chapter. Each could be a project of its own.

Close on the claim that this is about language effects, not language determinism. Language almost always works together with other factors, above all with policy. The book argues against cultural determinism about language, not against culture.

:::
